web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: Chapter 7: Why the Stock Trades Here — Market Expectations vs. Peers
question: What growth, margin, and dilution assumptions are priced into AMD at $387.65, and how does it stack up against NVIDIA, Broadcom, and semiconductor peers?

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get.
epigraph.author: Warren Buffett

web_blocks.title: 7.1 Deconstructing $387.65: Headline Multiples vs. Fully Diluted Economic Reality

web_blocks.html: On November 24, 2026, AMD closed at $387.65 on TradingView ($386.81 on the options feed) [28]. That gives AMD a $635.78 billion market cap ($628.88B on Finviz) and a $622.02 billion enterprise value [27][28]. On TTM revenue of $45.44B and GAAP net income of $7.62B, the stock trades at 84.26x TTM P/E (83.34x Finviz) and 56.05x EV/EBITDA [27][28]. Its 13.84x Price-to-Sales ratio sits more than double its 10-year average of 6.33x and 72% above its FY2025 average of 8.06x [31].

Bulls immediately point to forward earnings. Wall Street consensus projects Non-GAAP EPS jumping from $8.09 in FY2026 to roughly $17.64 in FY2027 as Instinct MI450 and Helios racks scale [29]. Against that $17.64 headline estimate, AMD appears optically reasonable at 21.51x Forward P/E [27]. Yet that headline multiple hides two massive economic drags uncovered in Pass 1 and confirmed on November 23, 2026. First, AMD's November 23 Form S-3ASR registered 336,934,324 common shares for potential resale by selling stockholders: 160 million OpenAI warrant shares, 160 million Meta warrant shares, 14.98 million World Labs closing shares, and 1.96 million Taalas shares [26]. If the OpenAI and Meta 6-gigawatt MI450 ramps succeed, AMD's diluted share count expands by roughly 20.5% toward ~1.98 billion shares. Second, Non-GAAP EPS strips out ~$1.8B+ of annual stock-based compensation and ongoing acquisition amortization while ignoring an $81.8 billion off-balance-sheet commitment stack [2][26].

web_blocks.title: 7.2 Fully Diluted Reverse DCF: What $387.65 Assumes at a 4.92% 10-Year Yield

web_blocks.html: The U.S. 10-Year Treasury yield sits at 4.92% as of November 23, 2026 [32]. A cyclical chip designer with $81.8 billion in off-balance-sheet obligations requires a 10.0% WACC. At $387.65 across 1.98 billion fully diluted shares, the market prices AMD at a $767 billion diluted equity value [26][28]. Yet FY2025 continuing-ops FCF was just $5.52 billion [1]. In 9M 2026, FCF was $4.68 billion (13.3% margin) as CapEx nearly doubled to $1.85 billion and inventory reached $11.46 billion [2].

Our Reverse DCF tests what $387.65 assumes after SBC and warrant dilution. To earn 10.0% annually over 10 years, AMD must grow revenue at 19.5% per year from $34.64B to over $205 billion by FY2035. It must also lift true ex-SBC FCF margins from ~13% today to 24% without a single inventory write-down. Our Base Case models $76.0B in FY2027 revenue at a 34.0% ex-amortization operating margin ($25.84B EBIT). Deducting $1.80B in SBC ($24.04B pre-tax) and 13% tax yields $20.91B in ex-SBC net income, or $11.31 per share across 1.85B weighted diluted shares. At 33.2x (a discount to Broadcom's 36.6x TTM P/E), Base fair value is $375.00, or 3.3% below today's $387.65 close.

web_blocks.title: Fully Diluted Reverse DCF & Base Fair Value Stress Test
web_blocks.the_number: At a 10.0% WACC (4.92% 10Y Treasury) and 24% terminal ex-SBC FCF margin, $387.65 prices in ~19.5% 10-year revenue CAGR across a warrant-diluted share base. Our reconciled Base Case fair value is $375.00 (-3.3% vs. CMP).
web_blocks.how_calculated: Base Case models FY2027 revenue of $76.0B x 34.0% ex-amortization OPM ($25.84B) minus $1.80B SBC ($24.04B) x 0.87 (13% tax) = $20.91B ex-SBC NI / 1.85B weighted diluted shares = $11.31 ex-SBC EPS x 33.2x = $375.49 (~$375.00).
web_blocks.sensitivity: Every 200 bps of gross margin erosion from HBM/rack-scale mix cuts Base value by ~$32/share; full 320M warrant vesting cuts per-share intrinsic value by ~16% unless incremental gigawatt revenue clears >30% operating margins.
web_blocks.the_inputs: US 10Y Treasury 4.92% (Nov 23, 2026), WACC 10.0%, FY2025 base revenue $34.64B, 1.85B weighted diluted shares (partial vesting of 320M OpenAI/Meta warrants + 16.9M World Labs & Taalas shares), 13% effective tax rate, 24% terminal ex-SBC FCF margin.
web_blocks.the_range: Bear $180.00 ($58.0B rev, 28% ex-amort OPM, $7.18 ex-SBC EPS x 25.0x) to Base $375.00 ($76.0B rev, $11.31 EPS x 33.2x) to Bull $540.00 ($95.0B rev, $14.98 EPS x 36.0x).
web_blocks.if_off: Every 200 bps of gross margin erosion from HBM/rack-scale mix cuts Base value by ~$32/share; full 1.98B warrant/M&A dilution at a 15x Broadcom forward multiple implies a $189 stress floor.

web_blocks.title: 7.3 Peer Valuation Matrix: The NVIDIA and Broadcom Problem

web_blocks.html: Peer multiples deliver the sharpest warning against chasing AMD today. On November 24, 2026, NVIDIA (NVDA) trades at 15.45x TTM P/E and 8.66x Forward P/E [33]. NVIDIA earns a 74.93% gross margin, 66.15% operating margin, and 74.23% ROIC [33]. Broadcom (AVGO) trades at 14.86x Forward P/E with 66.54% gross margins and 24.39% ROIC [34]. By contrast, AMD demands 83.34x TTM P/E and 21.51x Forward P/E for a 51.19% gross margin and 9.86% ROIC [27]. Both Marvell (MRVL) and Qualcomm (QCOM) also trade at wide forward discounts [35][36]. Paying a steep premium for the #2 AI challenger over cheaper, higher-margin leaders leaves no margin of safety at $387.65.

web_blocks.caption: Semiconductor Peer Valuation, Profitability & Stage Comparison (As of 2026-11-24) [27][33][34][35][36][37]
web_blocks.takeaway: Every major semiconductor peer sits in Stage 4, yet AMD carries the richest TTM P/E (83.34x), EV/EBITDA (56.05x), and second-richest Forward P/E (21.51x)—more than double NVIDIA's 8.66x Forward P/E despite trailing NVDA by 2,374 bps in gross margin and 6,437 bps in ROIC.

web_blocks.company: Micron Technology (2017–2018 Peak Cycle vs. 2019–2020 Inventory Digestion)
web_blocks.mechanism: During the 2017–2018 cloud memory boom, Micron's revenue surged 50% and bulls argued forward P/E multiples were cheap because hyperscaler demand looked secular. Yet surging industry purchase commitments and channel inventory caused margins to collapse once cloud buyers paused orders in late 2018.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Micron's stock fell >50% from $64.66 (May 2018) to $28.39 (Dec 2018) even as trailing earnings remained strong; GAAP operating margins compressed from 49% in FY2018 to 14% in FY2020.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: In capital-intensive semiconductor booms, headline forward P/E multiples look lowest right before inventory digestion or dilution hits. For AMD, $11.46B in inventory and $48.76B in supplier commitments create acute downside torque if hyperscaler AI CapEx pauses.

book_paragraphs: Before we ever look at a chart or think about placing a trade, you and I have to ask one blunt question: what is the market already assuming at $387.65? Because after a 41% plunge from $658.52, every instinct in your brain whispers that AMD must be on sale. That instinct is how disciplined investors get hurt in semiconductor cycles.

Let us look under the hood together. At $387.65, AMD is still a $635.8 billion company. It trades at 84 times trailing GAAP earnings, 56 times EV-to-EBITDA, and 13.8 times trailing sales—more than double its ten-year average sales multiple of 6.3x. Now, Wall Street bulls will tell you to ignore trailing GAAP numbers and look at 2027 Non-GAAP consensus EPS of $17.64, which puts the stock at 21.5 times forward earnings.

Hold on. That 21.5x multiple is an optical illusion unless you adjust for two giant footnotes we uncovered. On November 23, 2026—literally one day before our cutoff—AMD filed Form S-3ASR registering 336.9 million shares for potential resale. That includes 320 million penny-warrant shares tied to OpenAI and Meta, plus nearly 17 million shares from the World Labs and Taalas acquisitions. If the MI450 gigawatt ramp succeeds, your slice of the pie shrinks by roughly 20%. Suddenly, that tidy 21.5x forward multiple stretches toward 26x on a fully diluted basis, before even deducting stock-based compensation.

Now step back and compare AMD to its rivals sitting right next door on the trading screen. NVIDIA trades at 8.7 times forward earnings with 75% gross margins and 74% ROIC. Broadcom trades at 14.9 times forward earnings with 67% gross margins and 49% operating margins. Why would you pay a steep valuation premium for AMD—a cyclical #2 challenger with 51% gross margins, 18% operating margins, and $81.8 billion in off-balance-sheet commitments—when the category kings trade at half the multiple?

When we run a clean, fully diluted Reverse DCF at a 10% discount rate (reflecting today's 4.92% ten-year Treasury yield), $387.65 still demands nearly 20% annual revenue compounding for a full decade alongside a near-doubling of free cash flow margins. Our realistic Base Case fair value—giving AMD full credit for EPYC dominance and a strong MI450 ramp, while deducting warrant dilution and balance-sheet risk—lands at $375.00. Even after a brutal 41% selloff, the stock is not cheap enough to compensate you for the risk.

Let us walk through the Reverse DCF math step by step so you can see exactly why a 41% stock drop does not automatically create a bargain. Start with the risk-free rate. As of November 23, 2026, the U.S. 10-Year Treasury yields 4.92%. That is not the zero-interest-rate world of 2021. When risk-free government bonds pay nearly 5%, a cyclical fabless semiconductor company carrying $81.8 billion in off-balance-sheet obligations must clear at least a 10.0% weighted average cost of capital.

Next, look at the denominator: share count. Most retail screens divide AMD's market cap by 1.64 billion current shares. That gives you $635.8 billion on TradingView and $628.9 billion on Finviz. Now read the November 23 Form S-3ASR prospectus line by line. AMD registered 160 million warrant shares for OpenAI, 160 million warrant shares for Meta, 14.98 million closing shares for World Labs, and 1.96 million closing and contingent shares for Taalas. That totals 336,934,324 shares. If OpenAI and Meta actually deploy the six gigawatts of MI450 racks that Wall Street bulls are modeling in their revenue spreadsheets, those penny warrants vest. You cannot count the revenue in the numerator while ignoring the 320 million warrant shares in the denominator.

Watch what happens when you keep both sides of the equation honest. Across a 1.98 billion fully diluted share base, $387.65 implies a $767 billion equity value. Even using a blended 1.85 billion weighted diluted share count for our Base Case, AMD must compound revenue at roughly 19.5% per year for a full decade—growing from $34.64 billion in FY2025 to more than $205 billion by FY2035—while lifting true ex-SBC free cash flow margins from 13.3% in 9M 2026 to 24.0% sustainably. Remember how AMD got to 13.3% FCF margin this year: continuing-ops cash flow was $6.52 billion, CapEx nearly doubled to $1.85 billion, and inventory absorbed billions of dollars of working capital. Doubling free cash flow margins while financing $48.76 billion in supplier commitments and scaling lower-margin full-rack Helios systems is a very high bar.

Now run our sensitivity test. What if AMD grows at a still-impressive 17.5% ten-year CAGR—reaching $174 billion in annual revenue—and hits a 24% terminal free cash flow margin? At a 10% discount rate on 1.85 billion diluted shares, intrinsic value lands at $351 per share, nearly 10% below today's price. What if HBM memory inflation or rack-scale assembly trims terminal FCF margins to 20% instead of 24%? Even at 19.5% annual revenue growth, fair value drops to $344 per share. Only in the upper-right corner of the matrix—22% ten-year compounding at 24% to 28% FCF margins—does today's price look genuinely cheap.

That brings us back to relative value, which is the ultimate sanity check for any portfolio manager. You never invest in a vacuum; every dollar you put into AMD is a dollar you cannot put into NVIDIA, Broadcom, Qualcomm, or risk-free Treasury bills. On November 24, 2026, NVIDIA generates $361.8 billion in trailing revenue, $226.3 billion in net income, 74.93% gross margins, 66.15% operating margins, and 74.23% ROIC—yet trades at 15.45x trailing earnings, 8.66x forward earnings, and 13.98x EV-to-EBITDA. Broadcom delivers $89.1 billion in sales, 66.54% gross margins, 48.57% operating margins, and 24.39% ROIC at 14.86x forward earnings. Qualcomm trades at 13.41x forward earnings with 31.13% ROIC. Even Marvell trades at 16.85x forward earnings.

Ask yourself a simple, honest question: why is AMD trading at 83.3x trailing GAAP earnings, 56.1x EV-to-EBITDA, and 21.5x headline forward earnings—more than 2.4 times NVIDIA's forward multiple—when its gross margin is 24 percentage points lower and its ROIC is 64 percentage points lower? Because the market has been paying an option premium for AMD's 2027 growth rate. Look at our Micron Technology historical parallel from 2017 to 2020. In semiconductor booms, paying peak sales multiples (13.8x P/S versus AMD's 6.3x ten-year average) right as purchase commitments quadruple and inventory swells is historically how investors suffer 40% to 50% multiple compression. Our Base Case fair value of $375.00 reflects full respect for AMD's EPYC and MI450 execution while refusing to overpay for dilution and cyclicality.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Never Anchor to the 52-Week High
book_callouts.text: A stock that falls from $658 to $387 feels cheap only if you anchor to yesterday's euphoria. Value is set by future cash flows per diluted share—and AMD's November 23 S-3ASR filing reminded the market that 336.9 million extra shares are waiting at the exit door.
